Doctors and Patients Differ in Explanatory Artificial Intelligence Preferences During Diagnosis

In an exploratory investigation evaluating how distinct clinical stakeholders interact with diagnostic machine learning systems, researchers have demonstrated that physicians and prospective patients diverge markedly in the explanatory models they prioritize and value. Although deep learning architectures and convolutional neural networks demonstrate increasingly sophisticated predictive capabilities in oncology and radiological pattern recognition, their widespread clinical integration remains constrained by the black box dilemma. Because clinical algorithms frequently deliver diagnostic categorizations without revealing the underlying rationale that generated them, opaque recommendations risk compromising user trust, obscuring ethical accountability, and undermining shared decision-making. To examine how explanatory frameworks might be tailored to resolve these challenges, the investigators assessed how practicing clinicians and novice patient proxies evaluated four formalized explanation structures—causal, counterfactual, contrastive, and mechanistic—across sequential clinical trajectories involving cerebral glioma diagnosis and post-radiotherapy disease progression.

The study specifically conceptualized explanations through an established human factors framework that links explanatory typologies to the fundamental operational questions users pose during high-stakes decision-making. Within this taxonomy, causal explanations describe direct cause-and-effect mechanisms linking observed diagnostic markers to clinical predictions, answering fundamental questions regarding why a specific outcome occurred. Mechanistic explanations operate as an elaborated subset of causal reasoning, detailing the internal functional processes, cellular interactions, and physiological cascades through which multiple systemic components jointly produce observable symptoms. In contrast, counterfactual explanations adopt hypothetical reasoning by identifying the smallest alteration in input conditions required to produce an alternative classification, thereby clarifying what conditions would need to change to yield a different outcome. Finally, contrastive explanations provide comparative justifications by contrasting the factual outcome against an explicit non-occurring alternative foil, directly addressing why a particular clinical diagnosis was established rather than an alternative condition.

To rigorously contrast how professional expertise influences explanatory requirements, the investigative team recruited ninety participants via online survey platforms, ultimately retaining a cleaned analytical cohort of fifty-eight individuals following the exclusion of incomplete protocols and participant attrition during initial case screening. The final cohort comprised twenty-six practicing medical doctors spanning diverse clinical specialties—most frequently family medicine, diagnostic radiology, ophthalmology, and internal medicine, representing six nationalities with a mean age of 40.7 years—alongside thirty-two university students who served as experimental proxies for lay patients, representing eleven nationalities with a mean age of 21.9 years. Ethical review and formal protocol oversight were administered by the ethics committee of the University of Twente in the Netherlands. Statistical sensitivity calculations confirmed that the sample possessed sufficient statistical power to detect medium-to-large effects, establishing an empirical baseline for exploring adaptive explainable artificial intelligence architectures.

The experimental procedure placed participants within a simulated, two-stage sequential clinical trajectory derived from published neuro-oncology cases, portraying the primary diagnostic workup and subsequent post-therapeutic follow-up of a patient presenting with an intracranial neoplasm. In the primary phase, participants evaluated an initial diagnosis of a low-grade glioma supported by baseline magnetic resonance imaging and symptom presentation, completing nine standardized multiple-choice selection tasks across symptoms, diagnosis, and initial treatment. In the secondary phase, participants evaluated the identical clinical case three months following external radiotherapy, where clinical documentation and follow-up imaging indicated lesion expansion, cognitive deterioration, and progression toward high-grade malignant transformation, prompting another nine explanation-selection items. Crucially, the diagnostic scenarios and questionnaire items were systematically framed to align with stakeholder expertise, providing clinicians with formal physiological terminology and patient proxies with accessible, non-technical descriptions while holding core clinical facts constant.

For each of the eighteen standardized clinical questions, participants selected their preferred explanatory response from four options representing causal, mechanistic, counterfactual, and contrastive structures, immediately following which they recorded their subjective satisfaction with the selected statement on a five-point Likert scale. When examining selection frequencies through normalized within-participant response distributions, the researchers found that causal and mechanistic explanations accounted for the substantial majority of preferred responses across both stakeholder cohorts. For practicing clinicians, mechanistic explanations comprised 33.47 percent of selections and causal statements accounted for 32.64 percent, while contrastive explanations accounted for 23.07 percent and counterfactual selections represented 20.45 percent. Among patient proxies, causal explanations constituted 32.63 percent and mechanistic statements represented 31.11 percent of preferred choices, whereas counterfactual explanations accounted for 25.73 percent and contrastive statements comprised only 16.39 percent.

Statistical modeling using multinomial logistic regression with contrastive explanations designated as the reference category revealed significant behavioral divergences between the two cohorts. Compared to practicing physicians, prospective patients exhibited a significantly higher probability of selecting causal statements (beta = 0.417, p = 0.035), mechanistic descriptions (beta = 0.453, p = 0.024), and counterfactual alternatives (beta = 0.587, p = 0.006) over contrastive explanations. Clinicians demonstrated a greater proportional affinity for contrastive reasoning than patients, exhibiting a 6.68 percentage point higher rate of contrastive selections. Conversely, patient proxies selected counterfactual reasoning 5.28 percentage points more frequently than physicians. These selection distributions indicate that while both groups prioritize functional and mechanistic clarity regarding how disease processes operate, clinicians rely more readily on differential contrastive reasoning, whereas patients display an active aversion to comparative contrastive statements that fail to explain direct personal causality.

Analysis of participants’ evaluative ratings using linear mixed-effects modeling revealed critical insights into the relationship between explanatory preference and perceived utility. Across the entire sample, a Pearson correlation analysis demonstrated no statistically significant association between the explanation type selected and the resulting satisfaction score (r = 0.047, p = 0.146, 95% confidence interval [-0.017, 0.111]), demonstrating that a user’s intuitive selection of an explanatory style does not automatically guarantee high evaluative satisfaction. Although overall satisfaction scores trended slightly higher among patient proxies than among clinicians (beta = 0.407, p = 0.119), this general group disparity did not attain statistical significance.
